title: Roots
hookLine: Sariputta: the roots of the unwholesome are greed, hate and delusion; their opposites are the wholesome roots (MN 9)
last: SAMMA DITTHI — SEE IT AS IT IS.

cards: Anyone who's pulled weeds knows the trick. Snap off the top and you've done nothing; next week it's back, greener than before.
You have to get your fingers down into the soil and ease out the root, the pale stringy part you never see. Sariputta's first answer in his talk on right view is about exactly this.
Before the four truths, before the twelve links, he starts with actions and the roots they grow from.

teach.b: Kusala is usually translated wholesome, or skillful. In everyday Pali it can describe someone skilled at a craft, or someone well and healthy. Its opposite is akusala: unwholesome, unskillful.

Sariputta begins by naming ten unwholesome actions, a list later called the ten unwholesome courses of action: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will and wrong view.
Three of the body, four of speech, three of the mind. Then the roots. What is the root of the unwholesome?
Greed is a root. Hatred is a root. Delusion is a root.
And the wholesome? Abstaining from those ten.
And its roots: non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion. Sariputta doesn't stop at the list of actions. The ten are the weeds above the ground; the roots are what keep them coming back.
You can stop lying for a week by force of will, but if the greed or fear underneath is untouched, the lie grows back.
The wholesome roots are described with a not, but some teachers explain them positively as well: non-greed shows up as generosity, non-hatred as kindness, non-delusion as wisdom.
So a single generous act isn't only a nice thing done.
It's a root being watered. And why does Sariputta start here, in a talk about right view? Seeing clearly begins with seeing what's actually driving what you do.
Not to feel guilty about it. To know which root to tend.

how: Buddhist teaching across schools names the three unwholesome roots, greed, hatred and delusion, and the ten courses of action; some practitioners reflect at the end of the day on which roots their actions came from.

games.q: match each root to its opposite.

s: the ten unwholesome actions include actions of the mind
three of body, four of speech, three of mind: covetousness, ill will, wrong view.
Sariputta begins his talk on right view with the twelve links
he begins with wholesome and unwholesome actions and their roots.
kusala can also describe someone skilled at a craft
its everyday sense includes skilled and well.

games.q: you've told a small lie to avoid an awkward conversation. by Sariputta's teaching, what's worth looking at?
o: the root underneath it: greed, hatred or delusion.
games.why: Sariputta names the actions, then the roots they grow from; tending the root is what keeps the weed from coming back.

practice: Let the last day replay gently, and find one small moment you're not proud of. Without scolding yourself, look underneath it: was the root wanting, aversion or confusion?
Then find one moment you acted well, look under that too, generosity, kindness or clear seeing, and rest with that root a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Kusala. Wholesome, skillful: actions rooted in non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion, the roots Sariputta names first in his talk on right view.

orig.note: Pali kusala: wholesome, skillful; its opposite is akusala, unwholesome.

carryVoice: Your line: a root being watered. Every generous act tends one. Day three hundred fifty-five, done.

sources.ref: MN 9 (Sammaditthi Sutta), the wholesome and unwholesome and their roots
